title: UGSRC App
summary: Everything a University of Ghana student needs from their SRC, in one app.

meta.label: ROLE
meta.value: UI/UX Engineer, lead designer of the complete app

blocks.text: Important updates get missed.

The SRC IT and Innovation Committee says students miss them when they rely on WhatsApp groups, cluttered emails, notice boards, social media pages, and word of mouth [1]. 76,126 is the University of Ghana's official 2024/2025 enrollment, from the IRPO enrollment statistics [14].
I led the design of the UGSRC App end to end. That meant the whole experience, not a set of screens: how the app is structured, how people move through it, and how every feature connects.

items.title: Product structure.
items.text: Eight connected flows organized around one Home screen and five tabs.

items.title: End to end flows.
items.text: Sign in, find a pasco, ask a question, file a complaint, and follow it to a reply.

items.title: A connected system.
items.text: One set of components, colors and patterns shared by every feature, in four themes.

blocks.text: Problem: Official SRC information is spread across too many places, and students have no clear line back to the SRC.

The SRC's own IT & Innovation Committee put it plainly: students rely on "WhatsApp groups, cluttered emails, notice boards, social media pages, and word of mouth," so "important updates get missed, academic resources are scattered, and official SRC communication is not always easy to find" [1]. Even the university's Academic Affairs office says some students "still miss these essential updates" [2]. Past questions sit behind a library portal with a 48 hour registration wait, or in shared Drive folders [3]. Issues reach the SRC through one-off campaigns [4].

frame.alt: A student at the center of five channels: WhatsApp groups, cluttered emails, notice boards, social media pages and word of mouth, leading to missed updates, scattered resources and hard to find SRC communication
frame.caption: Where SRC updates live today. Source: UGSRC IT and Innovation Committee, in-app blog, Feb 2026.

blocks.text: Opportunity: Give the SRC one official channel that students can read, use and talk back to.

If the SRC owns one app, announcements are verified at the source, study material lives next to the news, and every complaint becomes a ticket someone has to answer. Students get one place to go. The SRC gets one place to listen.

frame.alt: The same five channels routed into the UGSRC App, which leads to Find it fast, Get answers and Be heard

items.title: Find it fast.
items.text: Updates, events, clubs, leaders and scholarships from one Home screen.

items.title: Get answers.
items.text: Past questions on demand and an AI companion for how-to questions.

items.title: Be heard.
items.text: Complaints, suggestions and questions, anonymous if needed, tracked to a reply.

blocks.text: Introducing the UGSRC App: the SRC, in every student's pocket.
One app for SRC news, past questions, campus answers and direct feedback, built on a single design system for students and SRC officers.

blocks.text: For this case study I pulled together what the SRC, the university and published research already say about how students get information.
blocks.checkNote: any SRC meetings, requirement docs or student feedback. If yes, add them here first.

blocks.text: What I found

items.title: Students already say the channels are scattered.
items.text: The SRC's own launch post lists five channels students juggle [1]. Academic Affairs started a WhatsApp channel because people miss notices [2].

items.title: WhatsApp is where students are, and it is noisy.
items.text: In a survey of 420 UG undergraduates, WhatsApp was the most used platform for academic purposes [5]. A 2026 survey of 454 UG undergraduates found "information overload and unequal participation" were the main problems with WhatsApp groups [6].

items.title: Past questions are essential and hard to reach.
items.text: The official route needs registration, a 48 hour wait and a second login per paper [3]. Students fill the gap with Drive links and unofficial sites.

items.title: Students have a lot to raise.
items.text: One SRC academic campaign collected 503 concerns, from results to scholarships [4]. In November 2026 the SRC and GRASAG told students to rely only on official SRC channels during a hostel fee dispute [7].

items.title: University services are split across portals.
items.text: MIS Web, Sakai, the STS portal and the halls portal each have their own login [8]. The university's earlier app, UGMobile, left the iOS App Store in 2024 [9].

items.title: One app with AI is where campus software is heading.
items.text: Platforms like Modo Campus and ReadyCampus sell one mobile front door with an AI assistant [10][11]. Georgia State's AI text assistant cut summer melt by 21.4% in a randomized study [12].

blocks.text: How it compares
Who I designed for
Hypotheses, not interviewed personas.

items.text: A fresher who does not yet know which portal does what.
A continuing student near exams who needs pascos fast, offline, on limited data.
A student with a welfare issue who wants to report it without being named.
An SRC officer who needs issues sorted and a way to reply.

blocks.text: These are the main decisions I weighed while structuring the app.
blocks.checkNote: earlier versions. Add real Figma explorations here if you have them. I have not described any discarded version that I cannot show.

blocks.text: One hub or separate apps.
Pascos, AI and feedback could each be their own app. I chose one hub so a student installs once and sees SRC news on the way to every task.
Chatbot or FAQ page.

A FAQ is easy to keep correct but hard to search. A chatbot is easy to ask but can make things up. I chose a chatbot that answers only from verified SRC and university documents and says so when it does not know [13].
Public or anonymous feedback.
Named feedback is easier to follow up. Anonymous feedback lowers the cost of speaking up. I made anonymity a toggle on every submission, so the student decides per issue.
Tab structure.

Five tabs: Home, PascoHub, Ujamaa, SRC Connect, Profile. Ujamaa sits in the center as a raised gold button because it is the one place you can start any question. Less frequent services (Clubs, Governance, Blog, Polls, Scholarships) live in Home's quick actions instead of competing for a tab.
Why one app?

items.title: One front door.
items.text: Email code to get in, then every service from Home.

items.title: One source of truth.
items.text: If it is in the app, it came from the SRC.

items.title: One loop.
items.text: Read an update, ask about it, respond to it, without leaving.

blocks.text: We designed a system, not just screens.

blocks.text: COMPONENTS

items.title: Color
items.text: Deep navy brand, mustard gold for primary actions, type colors for feedback (red complaint, purple suggestion, orange question), green status pills.

items.title: Themes
items.text: Light, Dark, System and Slate, all from the same tokens.

items.title: Navigation
items.text: Five-tab bottom bar with a raised center action.

items.title: Cards
items.text: Rounded content cards for updates, events, pascos, clubs and scholarships.

items.title: Chips and pills
items.text: Category filters, status (Open), level and semester tags, verified badges.

items.title: Bottom sheets
items.text: Feedback type picker, confirmations.

items.title: Inputs
items.text: One-time code boxes, search bars, toggle rows, chat composer with voice.

items.title: States
items.text: Success screens, empty states, loading, offline downloads.

blocks.title: How do 76,126 students speak up, get answers and study, when trust in information is the real problem?

blocks.text: CONSIDERATIONS

blocks.title: How do students raise sensitive issues without fear?
blocks.text: Anonymity is a toggle on every submission, and the issue still becomes a tracked ticket with an Open status and a thread, so anonymous does not mean ignored.

frame.alt: The Share Feedback form with the Submit anonymously toggle switched on

blocks.title: How does an AI assistant stay trustworthy?
blocks.text: Ujamaa answers from a curated set of verified documents, says plainly when it has no verified answer, and lets students report a wrong one [13].

frame.alt: Ujamaa replying that it does not have verified information, with an option to report the answer

blocks.title: How do pascos stay free to grow but fair to use?
blocks.text: A credit system: upload a reviewed paper to earn credits, spend credits to download. Downloads work offline for students on limited data.

frame.alt: PascoHub showing 39 credits available and an Upload and Earn Credits button

blocks.title: How do I keep study activity private?
blocks.text: PascoHub has its own sign-in by design, so a student's past-questions activity stays separate from their main account, as the app's privacy policy sets out [13]. A deliberate privacy decision, for one extra step.
blocks.checkNote: your rationale for the separate PascoHub sign-in, in your own words

frame.alt: The PascoHub sign-in screen, which asks the student to continue with their UGSRC account or use a different PascoHub account

blocks.title: How do officers keep up with volume?
blocks.text: Every submission carries a type and a category (Academic, Welfare, Facilities and more), so it can be routed to the right executive.

frame.alt: An officer view of an anonymous accommodation complaint with an Open status and a reply box

blocks.title: How do students avoid notification overload?
blocks.text: Students switch categories on or off and set quiet hours. Urgent announcements can still get through [13].

frame.alt: Notification settings with category toggles and quiet hours

blocks.text: Published on both the App Store and Google Play, but not yet open to students pending administrative checks.
The app is complete and running on University of Ghana infrastructure [13]. Because it is not yet open to students, there are no usage numbers to share, and I have not estimated any.
What I'd measure next

items.text: Weekly active students as a share of enrollment.
Time from an SRC Connect submission to the first officer reply.
Share of tickets resolved, by category.
Share of anonymous submissions.
Ujamaa questions answered without a "no verified info" reply, and answers reported.
Pasco downloads per exam period, and uploads approved.
Notification opt-out rate by category.

blocks.text: What I learned
blocks.checkNote: rewrite these in your own words. They are drafts based on what the work shows.

items.title: Design the system first.
items.text: With this many services, the hard part was deciding where things live. Once the structure and components were set, each new feature was quicker to design.

items.title: Trust is a design feature.
items.text: Verified content, an AI that admits what it does not know, and a ticket that always gets a status matter more than any single screen.

items.title: Anonymity needs a loop.
items.text: Letting students hide their name only works if they can still see their issue move.

items.title: Privacy can be worth a step.
items.text: Giving PascoHub its own sign-in keeps study activity separate. Writing down why that step exists makes it easy to defend, and to revisit as the product grows.
